judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The image is the page masthead, a wordmark reading "THE IRISH TIMES", with alt "Masthead logo". It is not inside a link, the page has no h1, and the small logo in the nav is aria-hidden, so this alt is how a screen reader user meets the publication name. The live page still uses it. The claim as worded, that the alt describes something the image does not show, does not hold: the image really is a masthead logo. The real 1.1.1 problem is different. The alt names the image type and leaves out the text the image shows (G94, close to F30), so it is not an equivalent. The element probably fails 1.1.1, but for a reason other than the one stated, and auditors could fairly split on whether the finding counts.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The image is an image of the word "ePaper" heading the ePaper promo box, with alt="logo". It is not in a link. The link next to it (the ePaper cover, a CSS background) has no name of its own, so this image is the only thing that says what the box is. "logo" is placeholder text, not an alternative (F30), and it does not convey "ePaper". Even if the image were treated as decorative, alt="logo" does not let assistive technology ignore it. The live page still has alt="logo". No passing technique applies.

judgments.label: true_positive
judgments.rationale: The "LIVE UPDATES" kicker link above the lead story. It is a section link, so it is meaningful text. The snapshot records the CSS colour #979797, 12px, weight 400, on a plain white background. The darkest pixels of the label in the screenshot are #979797, so this is not an anti-aliasing artefact. The live site CSS confirms it: --text-color-subtle is --global-neutral-4, which is #979797, with a font size of 0.75rem. That gives 2.92:1, below 4.5:1 for normal text. The text is not large, not disabled, not decorative and not a logotype, so no exception applies, and the page offers no high-contrast alternative.

judgments.label: uncertain
judgments.rationale: The element is a live-blog entry link (a > article > time + p) whose visible text is "1 hour ago The storm set to hit...". The snapshot shows that Chrome's accessibility tree gives the link an empty name. This fits Chromium not taking a name from content through an <article> descendant, so the claim that the browser computes no name is accurate. Against counting it: <a><article> is valid HTML, and accname's recursive name-from-content step (2F/2H) would take the name from the text. So the empty name is a browser implementation choice, not missing author content. Name computations like axe-core's give the text, and browse-mode screen readers (NVDA, JAWS) read the link content anyway, so "announces only link" is overstated for them. Focus or API-based announcements in Chrome may still lose the name. Competent auditors would split on whether this is a 4.1.2 content failure or a user-agent quirk.
